subject: Post-call: token economics, continuous batching assumptions, and next steps
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Ravi Shah <ravi.shah@azurahealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>, Leah Kim <leah.kim@azurahealth.com>
Date: 2027-04-28T13:10:00Z
Subject: Post-call: token economics, continuous batching assumptions, and next steps

Hi Ravi / Leah —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment before I send the formal cost model: 

Recap of what you shared
- Workload: real-time patient-facing summaries and clinician search signals (mix of short prompts ~20–80 tokens and longer context completions averaging ~600 tokens).
- Expected steady-state volume: 250M–400M tokens/month for initial rollout, ramp to ~900M over 9–12 months if pilot meets KPIs.
- Traffic pattern: continuous ingress with bursts at 08:00–10:00 and 17:00–19:00 local time; 60–70% of tokens during those windows.
- Latency SLO: p95 < 300ms for UI-critical completions; background batch reranks fine at higher latency.
- Security: VPC + HIPAA controls required (noted).

Unit economics goal you mentioned
- Target range: $800–$1,200 per 1M tokens for production (including reserved capacity uplift if needed).
- You asked for an example target at $/1M and an explanation of how batching/concurrency drives that number.

Key technical assumptions to confirm (batching & concurrency)
1) Continuous batching behavior: you expect steady continuous batching (not strictly per-request single-shot) and tolerate up to ~120ms additional batching delay for cost savings. Is 100–150ms acceptable as a batching window?
2) Average sequence length: we should model two representative buckets — short (25 tokens) and long (600 tokens). Please confirm % distribution; I used 55% short / 45% long for the first pass.
3) Concurrency: you plan to provision ~250 concurrent UI sessions at peak, with backend async workers for rerank/ingest. Does 200–300 concurrent inference streams sound right?

Proposed immediate next steps
- I’ll send a high-level cost slicer (attached spreadsheet) using the above assumptions with three pricing scenarios (hosted API decimal, reserved Dedicated uplift, and a Private deployment estimate).
- If numbers look right, we set up a 30-day pilot on dedicated share to measure real batch efficiency and token yield.
- Please loop in procurement for standard SOW/PO terms if you want us to draft next-week.

Action items for you
- Confirm the short/long token distribution % and whether the 100–150ms batching window is acceptable.
- Confirm peak concurrency range (200–300).

I attached the draft cost model (redwood_cost_model_AZ_v1.xlsx) — it contains worked examples at $/1M token points $600, $900, $1,200 so you can see sensitivity.

Thanks — happy to hop on a quick 20-min follow-up if useful.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Senior Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference
soojin.lee@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0192

Attachment: redwood_cost_model_AZ_v1.xlsx
From: Ravi Shah <ravi.shah@azurahealth.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: Leah Kim <leah.kim@azurahealth.com>, procurement@azurahealth.com, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-28T15:02:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call: token economics, continuous batching assumptions, and next steps

Thanks Soojin — useful recap. A few quick clarifications: 

- Distribution: updated figures look like 50% short / 50% long for initial rollout (we oversampled long prompts in the call — leaner now).
- Batching window: 120ms is acceptable for UI flows that are speculative (we display tentative suggestions), but for critical confirm flows (booking changes) we need <80ms. Can you show the cost delta when we force a sub-80ms latency SLA for 20% of the traffic?
- Concurrency: confirm 225–275 peak concurrent inference streams for UI; background async reranks use an autoscaled pool.

Procurement asked for a rough licensing expectation and a template SOW. I attached a one-page SOW template and procurement contact (procurement@azurahealth.com).

If you can provide a quick table that contrasts:
- $/1M tokens at 100ms continuous batching vs 40ms vs 20ms,
- and a row for reserved Dedicated vs hosted API for our expected volumes,
that would be perfect.

We looked briefly at the $800–$1,200 target — leaning toward $900 as the internal target if we can meet the <300ms p95 and demonstrate a 25% cost regression through batching during pilot.

Ravi

--
Ravi Shah
Head of AI Platforms | Azura Health
ravi.shah@azurahealth.com | +1 (617) 555-0110
Attachment: Azura_SOW_template.pdf
From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Ravi Shah <ravi.shah@azurahealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>, procurement@azurahealth.com
Date: 2027-04-29T09:20:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call: token economics, continuous batching assumptions, and next steps

Ravi — thanks, and appreciate the SOW template. I updated the attached model with the splits you provided (50/50 short/long) and added a table showing cost sensitivity at 20ms / 40ms / 100ms batching windows and effective $/1M token. High level findings: 

- With continuous batching at 100ms and the 50/50 mix, hosted API scenario arrives near $925 / 1M tokens (including networking & basic retention policy in the model).
- Forcing a 40ms window increases compute-cost by ~28% (effective $/1M ≈ $1,185) because fewer tokens are coalesced into efficient bursts.
- A 20ms constraint (needed for ~20% critical flows) pushes cost up ~60% relative to 100ms; we recommend a mixed routing policy: honor <80ms for critical subset on fast-path instances and route rest to batching-optimized nodes.
- Reserved Dedicated gives you per-1M effective cost improvements at scale — once you cross ~600M tokens/month the Dedicated uplift flips favorable: hosted at scale vs reserved shows ~15–25% savings depending on sustained concurrency and burst allowance.

I also included a quick pilot plan in the spreadsheet: 30-day dedicated trial, sample traffic generator for measuring token coalescing, and a PK/PO checklist for procurement.

Next steps I propose:
1) If procurement is OK, sign the SOW draft and we begin a trial (we can draft the SOW based on your template).
2) We run a 2-week baseline on hosted to collect real token-size distribution, then switch pilot to Dedicated share for 30 days to measure batching yield.
3) We deliver a final economic model and recommended routing policy (fast-path % and batching window defaults).

Can Ben and Laura join a 30-minute call tomorrow to walk procurement through the PO language?

Best,
Soojin

Attachment: redwood_cost_model_AZ_v1.xlsx (updated)
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
To: Ravi Shah <ravi.shah@azurahealth.com>, Leah Kim <leah.kim@azurahealth.com>, procurement@azurahealth.com
Cc: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-29T11:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call: token economics, continuous batching assumptions, and next steps

Ravi / Leah / Procurement —

Happy to run the procurement walk-through. Quick technical note ahead of the call: the mixed-routing approach above is exactly what we do for customers with hybrid latency needs — a small fast-path fleet (lower batching window, reserved if needed) plus a batching-optimized fleet. For your concurrency profile (225–275 peak), our pilot sizing recommendation is:
- Fast-path: 18–24 vCPU-backed low-latency instances (handles ~20% of peak traffic),
- Batching nodes: Dedicated GPU pool sized for 700–900M tokens/month with autoscale headroom for bursts.

I’ll have the preliminary cost/runbook slides ready for the call. Proposed time: 2027-04-29T15:00:00Z (30 mins). Let me know if that works and I’ll send a calendar invite.

Cheers,
Ben Carter
Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.ai
